newsitem.title: UK: Alleged IRA master bombmaker wins right to appeal.
newsitem.headline: Alleged IRA master bombmaker wins right to appeal.

text.p: An Irishman convicted of making a bomb that killed four British cavalrymen and seven of their horses on Thursday won the right to appeal against his conviction.
Gilbert McNamee was jailed for 25 years in 1987 of conspiring to cause a number of explosions, including the 1982 Hyde Park bomb attack on a ceremonial parade by the Household Cavalry.

The Criminal Cases Review Commission, in its first decision since it was set up earlier this year, referred McNamee's case back to the appeal court after doubts were raised about fingerprint evidence that was crucial to his conviction.

"Following enquiries into a number of issues, including scientific evidence, fingerprint evidence and the disclosure of evidence at the time of the original appeal, the Commission believes that Mr McNamee's conviction should be reconsidered by the Court of Appeal," the Commission said in a statement.
McNamee, who was described by the prosecution as the IRA's "master bomb-maker" during his trial, lost an earlier appeal in 1991.

He was convicted after prosecution lawyers told London's central criminal court that two of McNamee's fingerprints were found on adhesive tape found on a cache of bomb-making equipment found in woods in southern England. Another of his fingerprints was found on a battery used in the Hyde Park bomb which survived the explosion.
McNamee's defence lawyers had argued that while there were only two of his fingerprints on the tape, there were many more of someone else's there.
They said they had probably got onto the tape quite innocently when McNamee worked at an electronics factory in Ireland where rolls of the same type of tape were used.
Media reports also said that another convicted IRA man had claimed that he made the Hyde Park bomb.
If McNamee's appeal is successful, it will be the latest in a series of convictions for serious crimes to be overturned.

Since 1989, accused IRA bombers including the "Guildford Four" and the "Birmingham Six" have been freed after serving several years in jail, often after forensic evidence was found to have been unreliable.
The Hyde Park bombing marked the first big IRA attack after a lull of several years. Two hours later, another big IRA bomb in Regents Park killed another six soldiers and injured 30.
Both attacks were targeted at soldiers holding musical parades in the London parks.
The most famous survivor of the attacks was Sefton, a cavalry horse who needed an eight-hour operation to remove 28 pieces of shrapnel.

The Criminal Cases Review Board took over the Home Office's (interior ministry's) responsibility for considering whether to refer cases to the Appeal Court in March. McNamee's case was one of 253 passed on by the Home Office.
